"Your daughter," I say, voice low, "isn't the only one who knows the name of the safe house. She knows the code. She knows the timing. She knows the silence after the call."

I pause, fingers tracing the edge of the table. The cuff on my wrist is tight, but I don’t move.

"Next time, you don’t have to be so careful. She’ll be there. She’ll be watching. She’ll know what you did to the others."

I look at the floor. Not at her. Not at the cuffs. Just the space between us.

"Tell me what you did to her. Tell me what you did to her. I’ll let you go. But I’ll make sure she doesn’t forget."

The generator ran all night in the yard, coughing twice an hour like something that had learned the trick of breathing. By dawn the fuel was gone. Petra counted the jars on the shelf, then counted them again, and did not write the number down.

She came down to the river the way the year comes down to winter — slowly, and then all at once — and the water took her name and carried it, syllable by syllable, toward the sea that forgets nothing. And her grief was a fire that burned the low fields and turned the seed to ash before it could take root.

Their eyes meet across the yard. She looks away. His gaze follows her. Her eyes widen as he steps closer, and their eyes lock again. She watches him, and he watches her, neither willing to look away first.
